questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about regular languages:

S1: Every infinite regular language contains an undecidable language as a subset.
S2: Every finite language is regular.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- S1: an infinite language has uncountably many subsets, but only countably many are decidable. So some subset is undecidable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- S2: a finite language is a finite union of single strings [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true

questions.text:
For two n-dimensional real vectors [latex]P[/latex] and [latex]Q[/latex], the operation [latex]s(P,Q)[/latex] is defined as follows:

[latex]s(P,Q) = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n (P[i] \cdot Q[i])[/latex]

Let [latex]\mathcal{L}[/latex] be a set of 10-dimensional non-zero real vectors such that for every pair of distinct vectors [latex]P,Q \in \mathcal{L}, s(P,Q)=0[/latex]. What is the maximum cardinality possible for the set [latex]\mathcal{L}[/latex]?
questions.solution:
s(P, Q) is the dot product, so the set contains mutually orthogonal non-zero vectors. Such vectors are linearly independent, and [latex]\mathbb{R}^{10}[/latex] has at most 10 independent vectors (e.g. the 10 unit vectors).

Answer: 10

questions.text:
For a statement S in a program, in the context of liveness analysis, the following sets are defined:

USE(S) : the set of variables used in S
IN(S) : the set of variables that are live at the entry of S
OUT(S) : the set of variables that are live at the exit of S

Consider a basic block that consists of two statements, S1 followed by S2. Which one of the following statements is correct?
questions.solution:
In a basic block, control always goes from S1 straight to S2, so whatever is live just after S1 is exactly what is live just before S2: OUT(S1) = IN(S2).

Answer: OUT(S1) = IN(S2)

questions.text:
For constants [latex]a\geq 1[/latex] and [latex]b \gt 1[/latex], consider the following recurrence defined on the non-negative integers:

[latex]T(n) = a \cdot T \left(\dfrac{n}{b} \right) + f(n)[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct about the recurrence [latex]T(n)[/latex]?
questions.solution:
This is exactly case 1 of the Master theorem: if [latex]f(n)=O(n^{\log_b a-\epsilon})[/latex], then [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})[/latex].

The others are wrong in general: e.g. option 1 fails for a = 4, b = 2 (gives [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex]), and case 2 has an extra log factor ([latex]\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)[/latex]).

Answer: Option 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: if [latex]f(n)[/latex] is [latex]O(n^{\log_b(a)-\epsilon})[/latex] for some [latex]\epsilon \gt 0[/latex], then [latex]T(n)[/latex] is [latex]\Theta(n ^{\log_b(a)})[/latex].

questions.text:
Suppose the following functional dependencies hold on a relation U with attributes [latex]P, Q, R, S, \text{ and } T[/latex]:

[latex]P \rightarrow QR \\ RS \rightarrow T[/latex]

Which of the following functional dependencies can be inferred from the above functional dependencies?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]P\rightarrow QR[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]P\rightarrow R[/latex] (decomposition) True
- [latex]PS\rightarrow RS[/latex] (augmentation) and [latex]RS\rightarrow T[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]PS\rightarrow T[/latex] True
- [latex]P\rightarrow Q[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]PS\rightarrow Q[/latex] True
- [latex]R\rightarrow T[/latex]: [latex]R^+=\{R\}[/latex], so not implied False

Answer: [latex]PS\rightarrow T,\ P\rightarrow R,\ PS\rightarrow Q[/latex]
